pull request is where a team\\u0027s other humans join the loop, and QA is one of them. Today a task\\u0027s whole life belongs to one node: my node (or I, interactively) claim it, do the work, and the daemon opens the pull request. Everything after that is outside hall9k\\u0027s model except closeout monitoring. In a team project, where multiple people work the same repository (whatever the distributed shared-project system turns out to be), two pieces are missing.\\n\\nFirst, handoff. The work runs to the pull request on one node, and then it has to be handed to other humans. When the pull request opens, humans get assigned to it in GitHub, one or several, and each of them can take it on their own.\\n\\nSecond, what a reviewer\\u0027s participation is in hall9k\\u0027s own terms. A human doing a strict code review creates a pr-review task, which is the answer the platform already has. That task can be linked to the original task so the two are aware of each other, which is fine and is not the hard part.\\n\\nThe real kicker is QA. At ARX-5555 there is a QA team with no defined place in this loop, and the pull request is the spot. Today the pull request is strictly a code review: it gets reviewed, approved, and merged into main, and only then does the work become a Jira task for QA. QA picks it up, and the build has to be completed and deployed into staging and test before they can touch it. So main accumulates merged work that nobody has actually exercised.\\n\\nInstead, or in addition, two things happen during the pull request review phase, in parallel. One is the ordinary code review by another developer; in the concrete case, I assign my pull request to Sarah and she reviews the code. The other is a QA person reviewing the same pull request, but not as a code review. They review it as actual QA. They assign the task to themselves and claim it, which takes the claim away from me, and they pull. Hall9k sets up the worktree on their machine, gets it ready, and their machine runs it. They QA it in their own environment before anything merges to main.\\n\\nThe consequences are what make it worth building. Anything in main is releasable at any point, because nothing merges that QA has not already exercised. We can still keep a staging and test environment, but it stops being the gate. QA runs everything from their local environment and does not have to be a developer to do it, because hall9k does the setup that would otherwise require one. And if the QA person wants to write automated tests that belong to the repo, they add those tests to the branch: either as part of the same pull request, or as a stacked pull request sitting on top of the original one.\\n\\nThat also sidesteps a pile of infrastructure work. We do not have to figure out how Azure DevOps spins up a CI container and everything around it just to give QA something to test against. Maybe we still want that eventually, but in the meantime hall9k can do the setup for the QA person and we go from there.\\n\\nOpen questions for discovery, not decided here:\\n\\n- A claim today is per-machine and per-human, and a task reaches Done when the pull request opens. QA taking the claim after Done needs a story for what state the task is in while QA holds it, and whether QA is claiming the original task at all or a QA task of its own that is linked to it, the way a pr-review task is.\\n- Moving a branch and its worktree to another person\\u0027s machine is the peer-to-peer layer, which is designed and unbuilt. This idea probably cannot be built before that is, unless it takes a shared-remote path that does not depend on it.\\n- Stacked pull requests are not something the platform has any notion of yet.\\n- Whether a QA verdict blocks the merge, and if so where that verdict is recorded, given that the platform never
